transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

Cold, wet laundry after two hours is not normal. The leading possibility is a fault in the drying heat circuit — commonly the drying heater, thermostat or safety thermal cut-out. A blocked condensing/water path can also prevent effective drying, but that more often leaves the machine noticeably hot while the clothes remain damp. 1. Try a small drying load only — washer-dryers usually dry considerably less than they can wash, and the items should have been properly spun first. After 20–30 minutes, carefully check whether the drum/laundry feels at all warm. - Completely cold points strongly to the drying heater circuit. - Warm but still very wet points more towards condensation/airflow or drainage. 2. Ensure the cold-water tap to the machine is fully open and the inlet and drain hoses are not kinked. Many washer-dryers use a small flow of cold water during drying to condense moisture and then pump it away. 3. With the machine switched off and unplugged, clean the pump filter behind the lower access flap. Put towels and a shallow tray down first, then loosen the filter slowly. Fluff or debris there can obstruct the water used during drying. If it stays completely cold on a small, well-spun load with the water supply and filter clear, it will need an engineer to test the drying heater, thermal cut-out/thermostat, wiring and control. Those are internal mains components, so they are not a safe owner repair.

I ran a dry on a 4kg load and the door glass and drum stayed stone cold the whole time. No burning smell and nothing tripping. I can hear water trickling at the back during drying, and the fan is running. Do you think it's the heater then?

Yes — a drying-heater circuit fault is now the leading diagnosis. A 4 kg load with the drum and glass stone cold, while the fan runs and cooling water can be heard, is not an overload or normal poor-drying issue. The most likely internal causes are the drying heater element itself, its thermostat/thermal cut-out, or less commonly its wiring or the control board relay. A blocked condensing path usually gives a machine that gets hot but dries badly, rather than no warmth at all. One useful separator before arranging repair: run a normal 60°C cottons wash, not Eco or Quick, and check whether the door glass becomes warm during the main wash. - If it does warm up, the wash heater is working and the fault is confined to the drying heat circuit.
• If it stays cold on that proper hot wash too, there may be a shared heating/control issue instead.

I haven't tried a hot wash yet. I'll try a 60° cottons wash and see if the glass warms up. Anything else worth checking meanwhile? It stopped heating after I unplugged a drying cycle part-way through last week.

There is not much else worthwhile to check externally now. The 60°C Cotton wash is the useful next separator. Unplugging it part-way through a drying cycle would not normally damage the heater. It may simply be a coincidence, although a drying thermal cut-out can fail or trip after an overheating event; that still needs internal testing rather than resetting or replacing parts blindly. Cooling-water trickle and a completely cold drum, the likely fault remains the drying heat circuit: the drying heater element, its thermostat/thermal cut-out, or less commonly its wiring or control-board relay. A blocked condensation path would usually still allow it to become warm. If the 60°C wash heats normally, that strongly confines the problem to the drying heater circuit and an engineer can test those components. If that wash also stays cold, it points instead to a wider heating/control fault, which is still an engineer job.
Ok, I'll run the 60° cottons wash and check the glass. I'm happy to take the top off if that would help find the fault, though I've no multimeter. Would that be worth doing?

The likely parts are internal mains components; a visual look often shows nothing unless there is obvious heat damage, and the useful tests are electrical. 1. Run 60°C Cotton, not Eco or Quick, and check during the main wash or promptly at the end. - If the glass/laundry is genuinely warm, the wash heater is working. That makes this a drying-side heater circuit fault: most likely the drying heater element or its thermostat/thermal cut-out; wiring or the control relay are less common. - If it remains cold, there may be a wider heating, sensing or control fault rather than drying-only. A brief look under the top, with the machine switched off, unplugged and cool, is only worthwhile for obvious signs such as a loose plug, burnt connector or melted insulation. If you see any of those, stop using it and arrange repair. Do not disconnect or probe anything without proper testing equipment. Given the completely cold drying cycle despite the fan and cooling water operating, an engineer is the sensible route once that hot-wash result is known. They can test the drying heater, thermal cut-out/thermostat, wiring and control safely rather than replacing parts on guesswork.

Ok, I'll run the 60° cottons wash first and check the glass. I did take a quick look under the top before, I think there's a heater box with wires and a small round button-like part on top, but I can't tell if it's blown. Is that button thing worth worrying about?

It may be worth noting, but it is not something you can reliably judge by sight. The small round button-like item is often a thermostat or thermal safety cut-out associated with the drying heater assembly. It may look completely normal even when it has failed or opened, so its appearance does not confirm that it is blown. Do not press, bridge, disconnect or try to reset it: a thermal cut-out is a safety device, and bypassing it creates an overheating/fire risk. With the machine isolated and unplugged, only treat obvious scorching, melted plastic, or a loose/burnt connector as significant; if you find any, stop using the dryer function and arrange repair. Given the stone-cold drum during drying despite the fan and cooling-water trickle, the leading fault remains the drying heater circuit: heater element first, then its thermostat/thermal cut-out. The 60°C Cotton result is still the best way to separate a drying-only fault from a wider heating/control issue: 1. Run the 60°C Cotton programme, not Eco or Quick, and check during the main wash rather than after the final cold rinses.
2. If the glass becomes clearly warm, the wash heater is operating, which points to the drying heater, drying thermal cut-out/thermostat, or their connections.
3. If it stays cold, a wash-side heater/sensor/control fault becomes more likely as well. Without a meter, taking the top off further is unlikely to identify the failed component. An engineer can test the heater and safety devices safely rather than guessing.
